comments.text:
Jarred, ICE agents already have the ability to detain and arrest.

18 U.S. Code § 111 makes it a federal crime to forcibly assault, resist, impede, intimidate, or interfere with federal officers, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, while they are performing their official duties, with penalties ranging from fines and imprisonment (up to 10 years for using weapons or causing injury) to felony records. This law applies to actions like blocking agents, obstructing arrests, or getting too close during operations, even if motivated by protest, and can lead to serious federal charges beyond just simple assault.

ICE agents have authority under Section 278 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and related statutes to arrest non-citizens for immigration violations and federal crimes, but their authority over U.S. citizens is limited to situations where citizens interfere with their duties or commit federal offenses, like assaulting an officer, often involving coordination with local law enforcement under the 287(g) program for local officers acting under ICE authority. While ICE officers have broad power to arrest "aliens" without a judicial warrant, their actions against citizens are generally restricted to preventing obstruction or for specific federal crimes.
